questions.analysis: however 【线索】easy 与 much harder 形成对照 线索是同段相邻两句的对照关系：It's not difficult to set targets for staff. 用 not difficult 强调'容易'；It is much harder, __(1)__, to understand their negative consequences. 用 much harder 强调'更难'。一易一难，明显需要让步转折词。 【选项】A) therefore ✗ 顺承因果，与转折语境相反 B) however ✓ 完美承接 easy 到 hard 的反差 however 表让步转折：'设目标容易，然而理解其负面后果却难得多'。与前句的 not difficult 和 本句的 much harder 一一对应，逻辑严丝合缝。 C) again ✗ 表重复或再次，无重申语境 D) moreover ✗ 表递进同向，与反差不符 【验证】代回后：It is much harder, however, to understand their negative consequences.，整

Emphasize 【线索】上文 multiple components 与本句 others become distorted 互证 线索一在前一句：Most work-related behaviors have multiple components.——多维行 为有多个组成部分；线索二在本句后半：__(2)__ one and the others become distorted. 个，而非'识别/评估/解释'。下一段又用 Because the target is __(6)__. 进一步把'重点放在 【选项】 A) Emphasize ✓ 唯一能引起其他维度被牺牲的动作 Emphasize 表'强调、偏重'。只偏重一维，其余维度必然被忽视、扭曲，与 the others become B) Identify ✗ 仅是'识别'，不会让其他变形 C) Assess ✗ '评估'是中性观察，不导致扭曲 D) Explain ✗ '解释'仅是说明，与扭曲无因果 【验证】代回后：Emphasize one and the others become distorted.，与下段公交案例'只强调准

quickly 【线索】下文一连串反问把现象推到眼前 线索是紧跟其后的连珠炮式反问：Watch people get on and show their tickets. Are they carefully inspected? Never. Do people get on without paying? Of course!——只 【选项】A) nearly ✗ '几乎'弱化语义，与后文确凿现象矛盾 B) curiously ✗ '好奇地'引入主观情绪，与陈述基调不符 C) eagerly ✗ '热切地'再添情感色彩，同样不合 D) quickly ✓ '很快就能看出'与即时举证最契合 【验证】代回后：you'll quickly see how this works with drivers.，与后面立刻铺陈的多条现象呼

check 【线索】主语 inspectors 决定动作是'查验' 线索是主语：Are there inspectors to __(4)__ that people have paid? 主语是 inspectors Are they carefully inspected? 的 inspect 也作了同义复现的暗示。 【选项】A) claim ✗ '声称'不是查票员该做的动作 B) prove ✗ '证明'语义过重，需要前置举证 C) check ✓ '核查'正是查票员的本职动作 D) recall ✗ '回忆'语义对象错，不能用于他人是否付费 【验证】代回后：Are there inspectors to check that people have paid?，与前句 Are they carefully inspected? 形成 inspect→check 的同义复现，全段查票主题保持连贯。

ignored 【线索】整段主线'司机为赶时间而无视乘客' 线索是同段反复出现的'司机不在乎'现象：Are they carefully inspected? Never. 不查票； How about jumping lights? Buses do so almost as frequently as cyclists. 闯红灯。整 段语气一致——司机对乘客与规则都'置之不理'。下一段更点明 Because the target is 【选项】A) threatened ✗ '被威胁'施动方错，与情境不符 B) ignored ✓ '被无视'与赶点不停车完全对应 C) mocked ✗ '被嘲笑'引入情感色彩，与客观语气冲突 D) blamed ✗ '被责备'施动错位，乘客没做错被指责 【验证】代回后：And people who run for the bus? They are ignored.，与本段一系列'司机不在

punctuality 【线索】前句'晚点、班次少'＋后句'按用时奖惩'共同锁定准点 前句：People complained that buses were late and infrequent.——抱怨晚点；后句： drivers were __(8)__ or punished according to the time they took.——按用时奖惩。围 【选项】 A) punctuality ✓ '准点'与 late/time 双重对应 punctuality 表'准时性'。与前句 late（晚点）成反义对偶，与后句 the time they took 同主 B) hospitality ✗ '好客'与公交目标不沾边 C) competition ✗ '竞争'不是衡量司机的指标 D) innovation ✗ '创新'与公交场景无关 【验证】代回后：Because the target is punctuality.，与第二段'司机不查票、不接追车人、闯红 灯'反推一致——这一切都是为了准点；与下文 drivers were __(8)__ or punished according to the time they took. 亦顺承。

So 【线索】抱怨→对策标准因果链 线索是前后句关系：前句 People complained that buses were late and infrequent. 是'问题'，后句 the number of buses and bus lanes was increased 是'对策'。问题与对策 【选项】A) Yet ✗ '然而'引转折，与因果链相反 B) So ✓ '因此'精准衔接问题与对策 C) Besides ✗ '此外'是并列补充，缺前一项 D) Still ✗ '仍然'表让步重申，与对策不合 【验证】代回后：So, the number of buses and bus lanes was increased，与前句抱怨直接形成

rewarded 【线索】or punished 锁定'奖—罚'对照 线索是并列连词 or 后的 punished：drivers were __(8)__ or punished according to the time they took.——'按用时被___或被惩罚'。能与 punished 形成奖罚对照的，只有 rewarded（奖励）。 【选项】A) hired ✗ '被雇佣'与按用时奖惩无关 B) trained ✗ '被培训'非奖惩对照对 C) rewarded ✓ '被奖励'与 punished 完美对偶 D) grouped ✗ '被分组'与奖惩主题无关 grouped 表'被分组'。分组不是按用时考核的形式，与 punished 也无对照。 【验证】代回后：drivers were rewarded or punished according to the time they took.，整句

also 【线索】前句 hit these targets 与本句 hit cyclists 同动词不同宾语 线索是 hit 一词的双关：And drivers hit these targets. But they __(9)__ hit cyclists.—— 【选项】A) only ✗ '只是'排他，否定前面达标语义 B) rather ✗ '而是'用于纠正，需前句被否定 rather 表'而是、相反'。要求前句被否定再作补正，但前句'drivers hit these targets'是肯定句， 不能用 rather 翻转。 C) once ✗ '曾经一次'与一般陈述不符 D) also ✓ '同时也'把'达标'与'撞人'并置成讽刺 【验证】代回后：But they also hit cyclists.，与上一句 hit these targets 构成双关讽刺，与全文'达

revenue 【线索】措施'多查票员＋灵活定价'指向收入 线索是后半句：you would have more inspectors and more sensitive pricing. 查票员保 【选项】A) comfort ✗ '舒适'与查票员/定价无关 B) revenue ✓ '收入'唯一对应查票＋灵活定价 C) efficiency ✗ '效率'与本段时间维度重复 efficiency 表'效率'。其实质仍偏向时间维度，与下一句 If the criterion changed to safety 形成 D) security ✗ '安全'已被下一句占用 security 表'安全'。但下一句已用 If the criterion changed to safety 单独讨论安全，两者重复， 【验证】代回后：If the target was changed to revenue, you would have more inspectors and more sensitive pricing.，与下一句 safety/cautious drivers 并列形成'若改成另一种目标

cautious 【线索】safety＋obeyed traffic laws 双锁'谨慎' 线索一是前置目标：If the criterion changed to safety——以安全为标准；线索二是后置 定语：drivers who obeyed traffic laws——遵守交规。两者共同指向'谨慎、小心'的司机 【选项】A) friendly ✗ '友好'与安全＋守法不对应 B) quiet ✗ '安静'与安全主题无关 C) cautious ✓ '谨慎'与 safety 同义复现 cautious 表'谨慎、小心'。是 safety 的人物化体现，又与 obeyed traffic laws 完美对应。 D) diligent ✗ '勤勉'偏勤奋维度，非安全维度 【验证】代回后：you would get more cautious drivers who obeyed traffic laws.，与前面 safety 目标和后文 obeyed traffic laws 都贴合；并与本段下一句 But both these criteria would be at the expense of time. 共同表明'换标准换行为'。

problem 【线索】前文公交例已是'问题'，本句揭出另一个'问题' 线索一：冒号后 people became immensely inventive in hitting targets.——人们为了 题'。'另一个 ___'紧承上文，必为'另一个问题'。下段 Choose one criterion and you may well __(16)__ others. 也持续在谈副作用。 【选项】A) purpose ✗ '另一个目的'颠倒褒贬 B) problem ✓ '另一个问题'承接前文副作用脉络 C) prejudice ✗ '偏见'范围过窄、与目标无关 D) policy ✗ '政策'与冒号后行为不匹配 【验证】代回后：There is another problem: people became immensely inventive in hitting

noticed 【线索】对读者发问＋飞行常识＝'注意到' 线索是发问语境：Have you __(13)__ that you can leave on a flight an hour late but still arrive on time?——读者是乘客，被问的是日常飞行中的现象。乘客只能'注意到'这个 【选项】A) reported ✗ '报告'要求正式渠道，与读者口吻不符 B) revealed ✗ '揭露'要求主体主动公开秘密 C) admitted ✗ '承认'暗示不愿但被迫，与中性现象不合 D) noticed ✓ '注意到'最贴合读者日常感知 接给出解释 Airlines have simply changed the time a __(14)__ is meant to take.，完美承接。 【验证】代回后：Have you noticed that you can leave on a flight an hour late but still arrive

trip 【线索】前句 flight、后句 flight 双向夹击 线索一：Have you __(13)__ that you can leave on a flight an hour late but still arrive on time? 用 flight；线索二：A one-hour flight is now billed as a two-hour flight. 又用 flight。空里需要一个等于 flight 的上义词。trip（行程/出行）正是。 【选项】A) break ✗ '休息/中断'与飞行耗时无关 B) trip ✓ '行程'是 flight 的上义同义词 C) departure ✗ '出发'仅指起飞瞬间，不是整段耗时 departure 表'出发、启程'。出发只是一个时刻，谈不上'耗时多久'，与 time…take 不搭。 D) transfer ✗ '换乘/转机'是特定环节，非整段飞行 【验证】代回后：Airlines have simply changed the time a trip is meant to take.，与下一句 A one-hour flight is now billed as a two-hour flight. 同义复现 trip ≈ flight，论证清晰。

moral 【线索】后文直接给出'寓意'内容 线索是紧随其后的归纳句：Most jobs are multidimensional, with multiple criteria. Choose one criterion and you may well __(16)__ others.——这正是全文要传达的'教训/ 【选项】 A) moral ✓ '寓意'与后文主旨句完美匹配 B) background ✗ '背景'信息已在前几段，不在结论位 C) style ✗ '风格'与议论文主旨无关 D) form ✗ '形式'与议论性总结不搭 【验证】代回后：The moral of the story is simple.，下接 Most jobs are multidimensional, with multiple criteria. 形成'寓意—主旨'的标准结构，与 outline 中'第五段收束'吻合。

sacrifice 【线索】首段 distorted、第三段 at the expense of 持续指向'牺牲' 线索是全文反复出现的'牺牲'主题：__(2)__ one and the others become distorted. 用 distorted；But both these criteria would be at the expense of time. 用 at the expense of；but there is a __(17)__ 又再讲'有代价'。同义复现链指向 sacrifice。 【选项】A) interpret ✗ '解释'与牺牲主题无关 B) criticize ✗ '批评'与多维取舍无关 C) sacrifice ✓ '牺牲'与 distorted/at the expense of 同义闭环 D) tolerate ✗ '容忍'方向相反，弱化代价 【验证】代回后：Choose one criterion and you may well sacrifice others.，与首段 distorted、 第三段 at the expense of 形成'牺牲'三复现，主旨闭环。

cost 【线索】but 反差＋下句负面后果 线索一：Everything can be done faster and made cheaper, but there is a __(17)__. ——前肯定后转折；线索二：紧接的 Setting targets can and does have unforeseen negative consequences.——'有不可预见的负面后果'，正是'有代价'的展 开。'cost'与'negative consequences'呼应。 【选项】A) task ✗ '任务'与代价语义不沾 B) secret ✗ '秘诀'引出正面信息，与转折矛盾 C) product ✗ '产品'是具体物，与抽象代价不合 D) cost ✓ '代价'承前转折、启后负面 cost 表'代价、成本'。'但有一个代价'与下句 unforeseen negative consequences 同义复现， 【验证】代回后：but there is a cost. Setting targets can and does have unforeseen negative consequences.，'代价—负面后果'前后呼应，主旨闭环。

relating to 【线索】criteria 与 critical factors 是包含关系 线索：All good targets should have multiple criteria __(18)__ critical factors such as time, money, quality and customer feedback.——'多个标准 ___ 关键因素如时间、金 钱、质量、用户反馈'。标准必然'涉及/与…相关'这些因素，relating to 最稳。 【选项】A) leading to ✗ '导致'引因果，与并列因素不合 B) calling for ✗ '呼吁/需要'语义稍偏 C) relating to ✓ '与…相关'最贴合'标准涉及多个因素' D) accounting for ✗ '解释/占比'语义不合 accounting for 表'解释、占（比例）'。'标准解释关键因素'语义不通，且也不表'占比'语境。 【验证】代回后：All good targets should have multiple criteria relating to critical factors such as time, money, quality and customer feedback.，语义平顺，与 outline 中第六段'建议

specify 【线索】前文'好目标多维'＋本句'不止指明一两维' 线索一：上一句 All good targets should have multiple criteria relating to critical factors such as time, money, quality and customer feedback.——好目标应当多维；线 索二：本句 not only…but also 暗示'不止做 A 还要做 B'，A 是'指明一两个维度'这一步， 符合 specify 的'明确指定'义。 【选项】 A) specify ✓ '指明、明确指定'与维度搭配自然 B) predict ✗ '预测'与维度搭配不通 C) restore ✗ '恢复'前提是先丢失，文中无此前提 restore 表'恢复'。文中未提及维度被丢失，restore 无所对应。 D) create ✗ '创造'语义过宽，且与既有维度选择不合 【验证】代回后：The trick is not only to specify just one or even two dimensions of the objective, but also to understand how to help people better __(20)__ the objective.，

achieve 【线索】全文主旨'让目标真正达成' 线索一：第一段 Most work-related behaviors have multiple components. 暗示要让行 为整体都达标；线索二：本段 All good targets should have multiple criteria relating to critical factors such as time, money, quality and customer feedback.——好目标包含 【选项】A) modify ✗ '修改'与全文'达成多维目标'方向不合 B) review ✗ '回顾'缺乏 better 的努力方向 C) present ✗ '呈现'是展示动作，与目标实现无关 D) achieve ✓ '达成'是全文落脚点 【验证】代回后：but also to understand how to help people better achieve the objective.，回 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 以牺牲其他维度（安全、收入、质量）为代价。开篇即点题——It's not difficult to set targets for staff. It is much harder, __(1)__, to understand their negative consequences.，作 第一段抛出总论点（多维行为只强调一维会变形）：Most work-related behaviors have multiple components.；第二段以公交司机为例铺现象：Travel on a London bus and you'll __(3)__ see how this works with drivers.；第三段揭示成因——目标是准点：Because the target is __(6)__.；第四段补航空例佐证“为达标而变通”：people became immensely inventive in hitting targets.；第五段收束教训：The __(15)__ of the story is simple.；第六段 给出建议：好目标应当多维，参见 All good targets should have multiple criteria __(18)__ critical factors such as time, money, quality and customer feedback.。 SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 10 It's not difficult to set targets for staff. It is much harder, however, to understand their negative consequences. important to, It is difficult to 等），复用性强，是典型的常考句式代表。 Buses do so almost as frequently as cyclists. 第2段，第12句 If the target was changed to revenue, you would have more inspectors and more sensitive pricing. sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: "Reskilling" is something that sounds like a buzzword but is actually a requirement if we plan to have a future where a lot of would-be workers do not get left behind. We know we are moving into a period where the jobs in demand will change rapidly, as will the requirements of the jobs that remain. Research by the World Economic Forum finds that on average 42 per cent of the "core skills" within job roles will change by 2022. That is a very short timeline. The question of who should pay for reskilling is a thorny one. For individual companies, the temptation is always to let go of workers whose skills are no longer in demand and replace them with those whose skills are. That does not always happen. AT&T is often given as the gold standard of a company who decided to do a massive reskilling program rather than go with a fire-and-hire strategy. Other companies including Amazon and Disney had also pledged to create their own plans. When the skills mismatch is in the broader economy though, the focus usually turns to government to handle. Efforts in Canada and elsewhere have been arguably languid at best, and have given us a situation where we frequently hear of employers begging for workers, even at times and in regions where unemployment is high. With the pandemic, unemployment is very high indeed. In February, at 3.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent respectively, unemployment rates in Canada and the United States were at generational lows and worker shortages were everywhere. As of May, those rates had spiked up to 13.3 per cent and 13.7 per cent, and although many worker shortages had disappeared, not all had done so. In the medical field, to take an obvious example, the pandemic meant that there were still clear shortages of doctors, nurses and other medical personnel. Of course, it is not like you can take an unemployed waiter and train him to be a doctor in a few weeks, no matter who pays for it. But even if you cannot close that gap, maybe you can close others, and doing so would be to the benefit of all concerned. That seems to be the case in Sweden: When forced to furlough 90 per cent of their cabin staff, Scandinavian Airlines decided to start up a short retraining program that reskilled the laid-off workers to support hospital staff. The effort was a collective one and involved other companies as well as a Swedish university.

With the global population predicted to hit close to 10 billion by 2050, and forecasts that agricultural production in some regions will need to nearly double to keep pace, food security is increasingly making headlines. In the UK, it has become a big talking point recently too, for a rather particular reason: Brexit. Brexit is seen by some as an opportunity to reverse a recent trend towards the UK importing food. The country produces only about 60 per cent of the food it eats, down from almost three-quarters in the late 1980s. A move back to self-sufficiency, the argument goes, would boost the farming industry, political sovereignty and even the nation's health. Sounds great—but how feasible is this vision? According to a report on UK food production from the University of Leeds, UK, 85 per cent of the country's total land area is associated with meat and dairy production. That supplies 80 per cent of what is consumed, so even covering the whole country in livestock farms wouldn't allow us to cover all our meat and dairy needs. There are many caveats to those figures, but they are still grave. To become much more self-sufficient, the UK would need to drastically reduce its consumption of animal foods, and probably also farm more intensively —meaning fewer green fields and more factory-style production. But switching to a mainly plant-based diet wouldn't help. There is a good reason why the UK is dominated by animal husbandry: most of its terrain doesn't have the right soil or climate to grow crops on a commercial basis. Just 25 per cent of the country's land is suitable for crop-growing, most of which is already occupied by arable fields. Even if we converted all the suitable land to fields of fruit and veg—which would involve taking out all the nature reserves and removing thousands of people from their homes—we would achieve only a 30 per cent boost in crop production. Just 23 per cent of the fruit and vegetables consumed in the UK are currently home-grown, so even with the most extreme measures we could meet only 30 per cent of our fresh produce needs. That is before we look for the space to grow the grains, sugars, seeds and oils that provide us with the vast bulk of our current calorie intake.

When Microsoft bought task management app Wunderlist and mobile calendar Sunrise in 2015, it picked two newcomers that were attracting considerable buzz in Silicon Valley. Microsoft's own Office dominates the market for "productivity" software, but the start-ups represented a new wave of technology designed from the ground up for the smartphone world. Both apps, however, were later scrapped, after Microsoft said it had used their best features in its own products. Their teams of engineers stayed on, making them two of the many "acqui-hires" that the biggest companies have used to feed their great hunger for tech talent. To Microsoft's critics, the fates of Wunderlist and Sunrise are examples of a remorseless drive by Big Tech to chew up any innovative companies that lie in their path. "They bought the seedlings and closed them down," complained Paul Arnold, a partner at San Francisco-based Switch Ventures, putting an end to businesses that might one day turn into competitors. Microsoft declined to comment. Like other start-up investors, Mr. Arnold's own business often depends on selling start-ups to larger tech companies, though he admits to mixed feelings about the result: "I think these things are good for me, if I put my selfish hat on. But are they good for the American economy? I don't know." The US Federal Trade Commission says it wants to find the answer to that question. This week, it asked the five most valuable US tech companies for information about their many small acquisitions over the past decade. Although only a research project at this stage, the request has raised the prospect of regulators wading into early-stage tech markets that until now have been beyond their reach. Given their combined market value of more than $5.5 trillion, rifling through such small deals—many of them much less prominent than Wunderlist and Sunrise—might seem beside the point. Between them, the five biggest tech companies have spent an average of only $3.4 billion a year on sub-$1 billion acquisitions over the past five years—a drop in the ocean compared with their massive financial reserves, and the more than $130 billion of venture capital that was invested in the US last year. However, critics say the big companies use such deals to buy their most threatening potential competitors before their businesses have a chance to gain momentum, in some cases as part of a "buy and kill" tactic to simply close them down.

We're fairly good at judging people based on first impressions, thin slices of experience ranging from a glimpse of a photo to five-minute interaction, and deliberation can be not only extraneous but intrusive. In one study of the ability she called "thin slicing," the late psychologist Nalini Ambady asked participants to watch silent 10-second video clips of professors and to rate the instructor's overall effectiveness. Their ratings correlated strongly with students' end-of-semester ratings. Another set of participants had to count backward from 1,000 by nines as they watched the clips, occupying their conscious working memory. Their ratings were just as accurate, demonstrating the intuitive nature of the social processing. Critically, another group was asked to spend a minute writing down reasons for their judgment, before giving the rating. Accuracy dropped dramatically. Ambady suspected that deliberation focused them on vivid but misleading cues, such as certain gestures or utterances, rather than letting the complex interplay of subtle signals form a holistic impression. She found similar interference when participants watched 15-second clips of pairs of people and judged whether they were strangers, friends, or dating partners. Other research shows we're better at detecting deception from thin slices when we rely on intuition instead of reflection. "It's as if you're driving a stick shift," says Judith Hall, a psychologist at Northeastern University, "and if you start thinking about it too much, you can't remember what you're doing. But if you go on automatic pilot, you're fine. Much of our social life is like that." Thinking too much can also harm our ability to form preferences. College students' ratings of strawberry jams and college courses aligned better with experts' opinions when the students weren't asked to analyze their rationale. And people made car-buying decisions that were both objectively better and more personally satisfying when asked to focus on their feelings rather than on details, but only if the decision was complex—when they had a lot of information to process. Intuition's special powers are unleashed only in certain circumstances. In one study, participants completed a battery of eight tasks, including four that tapped reflective thinking (discerning rules, comprehending vocabulary) and four that tapped intuition and creativity (generating new products or figures of speech). Then they rated the degree to which they had used intuition ("gut feelings," "hunches," "my heart"). Use of their gut hurt their performance on the first four tasks, as expected, and helped them on the rest. Sometimes the heart is smarter than the head.

blocks.content: How to disagree with someone more powerful than you Your boss proposes a new initiative you think won't work. Your senior colleague outlines a project timeline you believe is unrealistic. What do you say when you disagree with someone who has more power than you do? How do you decide whether it's worth speaking up? And if you do, what exactly should you say? Here's how to disagree with someone more powerful than you.

You may decide it's best to hold off on voicing your opinion. Maybe you haven't finished thinking the problem through, or you want to get a clearer sense of what the group thinks. If you think other people are going to disagree, too, you might want to gather your army first. People can contribute experience or information to your thinking—all the things that would make the disagreement stronger or more valid. It's also a good idea to delay the conversation if you are in a meeting or other public space. Discussing the issue in private will make the powerful person feel less threatened.

Before you share your thoughts, think about what the powerful person cares about—it may be the credibility of their team or getting a project done on time. You're more likely to be heard if you can connect your disagreement to a higher purpose. When you do speak up, don't assume the link will be clear. You'll want to state it overtly, contextualizing your statements so that you're seen not as a disagreeable subordinate but as a colleague who's trying to advance a common objective. The discussion will then become more like a chess game than a boxing match.

This step may sound overly deferential, but it's a smart way to give the powerful person psychological safety and control. You can say something like, "I know we seem to be moving toward a first-quarter commitment here. I have reasons to think that won't work. I'd like to lay out my reasoning. Would that be OK?" This gives the person a choice, allowing him to verbally opt in. And, assuming he says yes, it will make you feel more confident about voicing your disagreement.

You might feel your heart racing or your face turning red, but do whatever you can to remain neutral in both your words and actions. When your body language communicates reluctance or anxiety, it undercuts the message. It sends a mixed message, and your counterpart gets to choose what signals to read. Deep breaths can help, as can speaking more slowly and deliberately. When we feel panicky, we tend to talk louder and faster. Simply slowing the pace and talking in an even tone helps the other person cool down and does the same for you. It also makes you seem confident, even if you aren't.

Emphasize that you're only offering your opinion, not gospel truth. It may be a well-informed, well- researched opinion, but it's still an opinion, so talk tentatively and slightly understate your confidence. Instead of saying: "If we set an end-of-quarter deadline, we will never make it," say, "This is just my opinion, but I don't see how we will make that deadline." Having asserted your opinion (as a position, not as a fact), demonstrate equal curiosity about other views. Remind the person that this is your point of view, and then invite critique. Be open to hearing other opinions.
